---
title: "Baseplane Integration"
---

## Architectural assumption

Baseplane is a subordinate library within the Cellerator conceptual and computational umbrella.

It is separate because sequence computation has distinct engineering needs:

- compact nucleotide encodings;
- validity and ambiguity;
- coordinate chunks and halos;
- bitwise predicates;
- reverse complements;
- motif and grammar scanning;
- CPU SIMD and CUDA bit kernels;
- sparse event or segment output.

That separation must not produce a high-friction boundary between sequence and quantitative state.

The intended system treats sequence, regulatory structure, expression level, and cellular behavior as connected domains and value planes.

## Ownership

### Baseplane owns

- packed nucleotide representations;
- validity-aware sequence views;
- reverse complement and strand logic;
- exact and bounded sequence predicates;
- motif and grammar programs;
- plane streams;
- bitmask generation;
- compact count, event, and segment output;
- sequence-local CPU, SIMD, and CUDA implementations;
- primitive-level performance contracts.

### Cellerator owns

- shared domain and order identity;
- cross-domain relations;
- sequence-to-regulatory joins;
- semantic execution geometry;
- physical projection construction;
- materialize-versus-fuse planning;
- quantitative state;
- regulatory propagation;
- training and learned weights;
- graph-wide execution and order;
- multi-GPU planning;
- persistence-image semantics.

### CellShard owns

- durable storage and transport of sequence or Cellerator artifacts when required;
- shard delivery;
- generation and compatibility;
- device staging.

## Dependency direction

Create a small shared ABI target:

```text
Cellerator::abi
    ↑           ↑
Baseplane   Cellerator core
                 ↑
       sequence integration kernels
```

`Cellerator::abi` should contain only stable, low-dependency contracts:

- identifiers;
- POD device views;
- status and validation codes;
- stream and device tokens;
- operand kinds;
- structure-builder sinks.

Baseplane should not depend on the complete Cellerator planner or runtime.

Cellerator may depend on Baseplane for sequence-capable builds.

## Current Baseplane strengths

The current Baseplane implementation already has the right low-level posture:

- two-bit sequence packing;
- packed 64-bit words;
- warp-native 32-base plane words;
- exact shifted-window scanning;
- count and compact emit;
- resident plane streams;
- base, GC, and CpG masks;
- caller-owned output;
- explicit CUDA streams;
- CPU, SIMD, and CUDA paths;
- no hidden allocation in hot APIs.

These should be preserved.

## Contracts to fix before freezing integration

## Validity and ambiguity

An unknown or invalid base must never silently become A.

A stable sequence view must carry validity:

```cpp
struct packed_sequence_view {
    axis_identity coordinate_axis;

    const std::uint64_t* low_plane;
    const std::uint64_t* high_plane;
    const std::uint64_t* validity_plane;

    std::uint64_t global_base_begin;
    std::uint32_t local_base_count;
    std::uint32_t word_count;

    std::uint32_t owned_begin;
    std::uint32_t owned_end;

    std::uint16_t left_halo;
    std::uint16_t right_halo;
};
```

Possible ambiguity policies include:

- invalid and never match;
- allowed-base masks;
- caller-certified canonical sequence;
- explicit IUPAC expansion.

The policy is part of the prepared predicate identity.

## Tail validity

Packed padding bits must not appear as A.

`local_base_count` and final-word validity are part of the view. Every predicate must mask its tail.

## Coordinate contract

Use bounded local coordinates plus a 64-bit base.

```cpp
struct sequence_domain {
    domain_id genome;
    std::uint32_t contig;
    std::uint32_t chunk;

    std::uint64_t global_base_begin;

    std::uint32_t local_base_count;
    std::uint32_t owned_begin;
    std::uint32_t owned_end;

    std::uint16_t halo_left;
    std::uint16_t halo_right;
};
```

Events use 32-bit local positions. The domain supplies global rebasing.

This avoids 64-bit position traffic in every event while supporting large genomes and distributed chunks.

## Prepared sequence programs

Public aggregate motif descriptors are too easy to construct inconsistently.

Use normalized immutable plans:

```cpp
struct prepared_motif_plan {
    plan_id identity;

    std::uint64_t low_bits;
    std::uint64_t high_bits;
    std::uint64_t validity_mask;

    std::uint64_t reverse_low_bits;
    std::uint64_t reverse_high_bits;

    std::uint32_t motif_length;
    std::uint16_t mismatch_limit;
    std::uint16_t rule_id;

    strand_policy strand;
    ambiguity_policy ambiguity;

    std::uint16_t required_halo;
    std::uint16_t flags;
};
```

The preparation step validates:

- motif length;
- active fields;
- mismatch bounds;
- reverse complement;
- palindrome deduplication;
- strand semantics;
- ambiguity;
- required halo;
- compatible output modes.

Count, mask, and emit consume the same plan.

## Output kinds

Baseplane should expose the representation natural to the result.

### Count

Use when only the total is needed.

### Bit plane

Use for dense Boolean predicates:

- base identity;
- GC;
- CpG starts;
- common motif class;
- accessibility gate over sequence coordinates.

One bit represents one coordinate or one logical window.

### Event stream

Use for sparse occurrences.

```cpp
struct sequence_event_stream_view {
    sequence_domain domain;
    std::uint64_t event_count;

    const std::uint32_t* local_position;
    const std::uint16_t* rule_id;
    const std::uint8_t* score_or_mismatches;
    const std::uint8_t* strand;

    event_order order;
};
```

Structure-of-arrays permits Cellerator consumers to read only required fields.

### Segment stream

Use for runs or regions.

```cpp
struct sequence_segment_stream_view {
    sequence_domain domain;
    std::uint64_t segment_count;

    const std::uint32_t* begin;
    const std::uint32_t* end;
    const std::uint32_t* class_id;
    const std::uint32_t* payload_offset;
};
```

### Direct reduction

When the consumer needs only counts or weighted sums per interval, Baseplane should support a segmented output sink rather than materializing every event.

## Event emission regimes

One global atomic append per event is not universal.

### Sparse unordered

Use direct or warp-aggregated atomic reservation.

### Moderate density

Use block-local compaction and one block reservation.

### Dense or stable order

Use:

```text
count per block
    → prefix scan
    → deterministic emit
```

Every result reports:

- total matches;
- records stored;
- records dropped;
- output capacity;
- ordering mode.

## Common operand view

Cellerator should consume Baseplane results through the shared operand vocabulary.

```cpp
biological_operand_view operand;

operand.kind = operand_kind::bit_plane;
// or event_stream, segment_stream, sparse_relation
```

No conversion to a dense byte tensor is required.

## Relation builder

Baseplane may write sequence-derived relationships into a neutral Cellerator builder.

```cpp
struct relation_builder_sink {
    domain_id source;
    domain_id destination;

    device_span<std::uint32_t> source_ids;
    device_span<std::uint32_t> destination_ids;
    device_span<std::uint16_t> rule_ids;
    device_span<std::uint8_t> attributes;

    device_counter count;
};
```

Possible outputs include:

- motif occurrence to regulatory element;
- sequence interval to chromatin domain;
- motif grammar to enhancer;
- variant to affected motif;
- sequence feature to gene promoter.

CellPack then compiles the resulting relation.

Baseplane should not know the bytes of a CP-BP physical projection.

## Interval joins

A sequence event must be mapped into regulatory domains without a host table round trip.

For sorted events and intervals, use:

- merge path;
- two-level genomic bins;
- bounded interval indices;
- cooperative search.

For unordered event emission, the planner may choose:

- stable Baseplane emission;
- device bucket by genomic bin;
- a consumer that tolerates unordered events.

The decision depends on reuse and event density.

## Materialize or fuse

The planner compares two routes.

### Materialized

\[
C_{\text{materialized}}
=
C_{\text{predicate}}
+
C_{\text{emit}}
+
C_{\text{relation build}}
+
R C_{\text{consume}}
\]

### Fused

\[
C_{\text{fused}}
=
R
\left(
C_{\text{predicate in consumer}}
+
C_{\text{consumer}}
\right)
\]

Materialization usually wins when:

- sequence is static;
- results are reused across many cells or time points;
- several downstream operations consume them;
- the materialized relation is compact;
- predicate evaluation is expensive.

Fusion usually wins when:

- the result is used once;
- only a small requested subset matters;
- event materialization would be large;
- the predicate can be evaluated while relevant sequence words are already resident;
- downstream accumulation can occur immediately.

## Fusion mechanisms

Use three levels.

### Precompiled fused primitives

For common paths:

- motif mask plus accessibility gate;
- motif event plus interval join;
- motif event plus regulatory accumulation;
- variant predicate plus local target update.

### Bounded sequence-program image

A small immutable device program may encode a limited set of prepared predicates and outputs.

The interpreter must remain bounded and specialized. It should not become a general virtual machine in every hot kernel.

### Optional JIT specialization

Highly reused unusual sequence programs may justify JIT or device-link-time specialization.

JIT is an optimization layer, not the stable persistence ABI.

## Example fused kernel

```text
warp loads packed sequence words
    ↓
computes motif match masks
    ↓
applies validity, strand, and optional chromatin mask
    ↓
enumerates active hits with ballot and bit scans
    ↓
maps positions to regulatory elements
    ↓
groups equal target identities with match operations
    ↓
multiplies by TF or learned state
    ↓
accumulates directly into element or gene state
```

Useful GPU mechanisms include:

- warp ballots for match masks;
- `__ffs` or bit iteration;
- `__match_any_sync` for equal targets;
- warp-aggregated atomics;
- shared genomic-bin indices;
- segmented reductions;
- compact device queues.

The biological regularity is the reuse of sequence predicates and target relations.

## Static sequence as a structural program

For repeated cellular computation, compile sequence once.

```text
immutable DNA
    ↓ Baseplane
motif and grammar structure
    ↓ Cellerator relation builder
motif-to-element or motif-to-gene relation
    ↓ CellPack
semantic geometry and projections
    ↓ repeated Cellerator execution
dynamic accessibility, TF activity, expression, and learned values
```

This is the preferred route for fixed genomes.

## Sequence-conditioned numerical operations

Baseplane outputs can act directly as:

- masks over Cellerator tiles;
- gates over module execution;
- sparse relation structure;
- event sources;
- segment membership;
- quantization or precision selectors;
- conditional work-queue producers.

A bit plane and a floating-point value plane may participate in one fused kernel without converting the bit plane to floats.

## Sequence-domain identity

A sequence operand must identify:

- genome or assembly;
- contig;
- coordinate convention;
- chunk;
- global base;
- owned range;
- halo;
- order;
- validity policy;
- sequence generation when mutable.

A regulatory relation must bind the exact source sequence domain and destination regulatory domain.

Same coordinate length is not enough.

## Multi-GPU sequence partitioning

Partition sequence by contig or bounded coordinate chunk.

The compiler records:

- owned interval;
- left and right halo;
- cross-boundary motif requirements;
- event ownership;
- target relation partition;
- replication or communication.

A hit belongs to exactly one owner even when its motif window touches a halo.

The static relation may later be repartitioned by regulatory module or target gene for repeated state execution.

## Persistence

Baseplane persistence should remain representation-specific and compact.

Cellerator execution images may reference:

- sequence domain identities;
- prepared sequence-program identities;
- persisted mask or event sections;
- sequence-derived relation sections.

CellShard may store and deliver these sections as opaque payloads.

Do not require Baseplane to adopt CPK1 or a future Cellerator physical tile format.

## Planner capabilities

Baseplane exposes capabilities such as:

```text
predicate → count
predicate → bit plane
predicate → event stream
predicate → segment stream
predicate + interval join → relation
predicate + relation + value plane → numerical accumulation
```

Each capability reports:

- supported sequence representation;
- validity policy;
- output order;
- workspace;
- deterministic behavior;
- expected output-density regime;
- architecture support;
- materialization bytes;
- persistent preparation.

Cellerator's planner chooses among them with downstream cost included.

## Integration acceptance criteria

The Baseplane-to-Cellerator boundary is ready when:

- invalid and tail bases cannot create false matches;
- coordinate and halo identity is explicit;
- sequence plans are immutable and normalized;
- masks, events, segments, and relations use shared domain identity;
- at least one materialized sequence-to-regulatory path remains device-resident;
- at least one fused path avoids an intermediate;
- the planner can compare those paths;
- static sequence structure can be reused across dynamic state evaluations;
- no dense one-hot or byte-per-base representation appears in the normal hot path;
- sequence and state operations can share a prepared Cellerator program.

The result should feel like one execution system with two specialized vocabularies, not two libraries exchanging exported tables.
